chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from al-Hakam ibn 'Utbah said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): What do you say about a domestic pigeon that was slaughtered in the miqat (open land) and then brought into the Haram (sanctuary)? He said: 'There is no harm in eating it for one who is in the state of ihram (muhrim), but if one is in the state of ihram, then no (it is not eaten).' And he said: 'If it was brought into the Haram and slaughtered there, then it was slaughtered after it had entered its place of safety (i.e., the Haram boundary).'

key_terms.مُحِلًّا: one who is not in the state of ihram
key_terms.مُحْرِمًا: one in the state of ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating a bird slaughtered outside the Haram but brought inside by a pilgrim in ihram?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Baqir clarifies the distinction between the location of slaughter and the state of the pilgrim, ruling that a pigeon slaughtered in the open country (al-Hill) remains permissible for consumption even if brought into the Haram, as the act of slaughter occurred outside the sanctuary. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that the validity of the meat depends on the place of slaughter rather than the location of consumption, provided the pilgrim was not in a state that prohibited the specific act at the time of slaughter. The hadith further notes that if slaughtered inside the Haram, it is considered valid because the animal entered the 'safety' (ma'man) of the sanctuary before the slaughter, distinguishing it from cases where the prohibition applies.
